name: Sandalwood paste sun protection

card.summary: A traditional South Asian paste of ground sandalwood, applied to the skin to cool it and shield it from the sun, which users link to a calmer, clearer complexion.
card.note: Not a tested sunscreen; sandalwood and related ingredients can cause contact allergy or pigmented contact dermatitis in some people.

quick.overview:
Sandalwood paste is made by grinding sandalwood on a stone slab with a little water until it thickens, then spreading it on the face or body. In South Asia it is used for its cooling feel, its scent, and as a traditional skin protectant against the sun.

People use it for a smoother, more even-looking complexion and to guard against sun darkening. The closest studied relative is Myanmar's thanaka paste, where laboratory work found UV-absorbing compounds; no published trial has measured the sun protection factor of sandalwood paste itself.
quick.how: Dry sandalwood is rubbed on a slab with water to form a paste, sometimes mixed with saffron, turmeric or other herbs and applied as a mask or all-over layer, then left on or washed off. Users describe it as part of a daily or weekly routine.
quick.risks: Reported problems are mainly skin reactions. Indian dermatology clinics have documented pigmented contact dermatitis from fragrances and plant ingredients identified by patch testing, and a study of home remedies in children recorded traditional preparations in skin care. People with sensitive skin or fragrance allergy are generally advised to patch test.

lead: Sandalwood paste is a traditional preparation in South Asia, made by grinding sandalwood against a stone with water into a cool, fragrant paste. It is applied to the skin in religious and everyday settings; for example, it is applied after the tonsure ritual at Tirupati to protect the skin [1].

People use it to soothe sun-exposed skin and to keep the complexion looking even and bright. Sandalwood's main aromatic components are the santalol isomers, roughly 75 percent of the wood's oil [1]. A similar bark paste, Myanmar's thanaka, has laboratory data showing UV absorption [2].

No published study has measured the sun protection of sandalwood paste on skin. Related literature includes dermatology reports on contact reactions to traditional and cosmetic ingredients in India [3][4].

chain: Cooling paste forms a layer on skin
Traditionally used to blunt sun exposure
Skin looks less sun-darkened and more even
angle.text: Users apply it as a cooling, scented mask they expect to protect the face from sun and to leave it looking smoother. The protection is traditional rather than measured.

paras: The paste is made by grinding dry sandalwood on a stone slab while slowly adding water; it is called kalabham in Malayalam and gandha in Kannada. Mixed with saffron it becomes chandanam, and further additions of herbs and perfumes give javadhu [1]. Devotees also apply it to the forehead, neck and chest [1].

Santalol isomers make up about 75 percent of the main sandalwood components; Indian sandalwood oil has a higher alpha-santalol content than Australian oil. Steam distillation is the usual way to extract the oil [1].

Thanaka, a paste from ground Murraya bark used in Myanmar for at least nine centuries, has a scent similar to sandalwood and is worn for its cooling feel and sun protection. A 2004 study proposed marmesin as a UV-absorbing compound, and a 2010 study reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and tyrosinase-inhibiting properties [2].

An Indian retrospective patch-testing study of pigmented contact dermatitis examined which allergens caused skin darkening in patients [3]. An observational study of 150 children recorded the home remedies caregivers used for skin conditions in the Indian subcontinent [4].
No studies found. Related work: thanaka has laboratory UV-absorption data [2], and patch-testing studies describe contact reactions in Indian patients [3].
